rubric.label: Real pain
rubric.help: Do people already spend money or hours on this problem today?

rubric.label: Clear payer
rubric.help: Can you name who pays, and roughly how much?

rubric.label: Your edge
rubric.help: What do you have that a random competitor doesn't (skills, access, network, taste)?

rubric.label: Room in market
rubric.help: 5 = wide open, 1 = crowded with cheap or free substitutes.

rubric.label: Speed to first krona
rubric.help: 5 = could get paid within a month, 1 = a year or more.

rubric.label: Life fit
rubric.help: Does it suit your job, the Vietnam stint, your writing and energy?

stages.name: Hunch
stages.test: Write the one-sentence pitch: who, what pain, what they pay.

stages.name: Desk research
stages.test: Competitors, prices and substitutes mapped. Rubric scored honestly.

stages.name: Conversations
stages.test: Five real potential buyers talked to. At least two say 'I'd pay for that' unprompted.

stages.name: Smoke test
stages.test: A concrete offer with a price is put in front of people (page, DM, pitch). Someone tries to buy.

stages.name: First money
stages.test: One paying customer, at a price that isn't a favour.

stages.name: Survived
stages.test: Repeatable: a second and third customer came without heroic effort.

ideas.name: AI adoption for small teams
ideas.pitch: Workshops, workflow redesign and small internal tools for 20–250 person companies that pay for AI tools but don't use them well.
ideas.verdict: The struggle is real and measurable: two thirds of Swedish firms use no AI, and those that hold back cite lack of expertise first. The market is crowded at the enterprise top and at the cheap-freelancer bottom. The durable product isn't tool tips, which go stale monthly, but workflow redesign, policy and an ongoing retainer to keep a team current. Knowledge going stale is the reason a retainer makes sense, not a reason to avoid this. Expect a 3–5 year window before tools get easy enough that small firms can do it themselves.
edge: Real building track record: CV app, review tools, footage pipelines, event sites
Video production and events background, a niche you can speak to credibly
Swedish and Vietnamese, plus access to Vietnamese-Swedish business owners
Your own workplace can be the first case study

competitors.who: Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG, Capgemini/Sogeti, Knowit, Netlight, Tietoevry
competitors.note: Enterprise budgets (hundreds of thousands of SEK and up). Rarely bother with a 15-person company.

competitors.who: Alice Labs, PhaseOne.ai, Lampo AI Automation, Opsio, Nytta AI (Växjö)
competitors.note: A data vendor counts about 192 AI consulting firms based in Sweden (Aug 2026), with Stockholm the largest hub. Several target SMEs directly.

competitors.who: NobleProg, Active Solution, Hyper Island and Berghs courses, Microsoft Copilot partners
competitors.note: Workshops and courses, often generic and not built around the client's own tasks.
AI & ML is one of Upwork's most-bid subcategories. n8n specialists charge roughly $40–100/h. Price pressure is strong here.

competitors.who: YouTube, an internal 'AI champion', the vendors' own onboarding
competitors.note: The real competitor for small firms is often 'we'll figure it out ourselves'.

ideas.pricing: Swedish AI consultants are typically quoted at 1,200–2,500 SEK/h (Opsio). Tool seats cost roughly 200–700 SEK per user per month. A half-day team workshop is the easiest first sale.
risks: Knowledge goes stale within months. Answer: sell outcomes and a quarterly refresh retainer, not a one-off course. Teach the method (pick a task, redesign it, measure), which stays useful whichever tool wins.
The window may close in 3–5 years as vendors (Copilot, Gemini in Workspace) build onboarding into the tools
Firms under 20 staff are adopting slowly, so they're the hardest to sell to; 20–250 staff is the sweet spot
Mostly a sales job: meetings, follow-ups, proposals
Conflict of interest or contract terms with your current employer: check before selling on the side
ideas.next: Run one internal pilot at work: pick one team and one painful workflow, measure hours before and after, and write it up as a one-page case study. Target 20–250 person firms after that.

market: Sweden 2025 (SCB): 35% of firms with 10+ staff use some AI, up from 25% in 2024. By size: small (10–49) 30.8%, medium 49.6%, large 71.9%.
65% of Swedish firms used no AI in 2025, and 57.9% neither used it nor considered it.
Among Swedish firms that considered AI but didn't adopt it, the top reason was lack of relevant expertise (74.7%).
The EU average is 20% (2025), up from 13.5% in 2024. Sweden is third behind Denmark (42%) and Finland (37.8%).
US (Census, 2026): about 18–20% of firms use AI. Use is rising at firms with 20+ staff but is flat at firms under 20.
Depth: most big companies use AI somewhere, but only about a third are scaling it. 48% added AI without redesigning the workflow (Deloitte 2026), and only 12% have redesigned at scale.

Workers are ahead of their employers: 89% use AI at work (Study.com), 41% say their employer gave no tools, training or guidance (Resume Now), and 35% of AI-using SMBs found unapproved AI running in their business (Pax8).
The gap is between individual use (high) and company adoption (low). The bottleneck is expertise and workflow redesign, not access to tools.

ideas.name: Footage logger for wedding videographers
ideas.pitch: Upload a day of clips and get a searchable inventory, transcripts of speeches and vows, and a beat-timed rough cut list.
ideas.verdict: Strong edge: you've already built the core for two wedding films. Needs competitor research, since editing suites are adding AI features fast.
edge: Working pipeline from the Jennie & Gunnar and Emma projects
You understand how an editor actually works through a wedding day
risks: Premiere, DaVinci Resolve and Descript may ship the same features as part of their own products
Video upload and processing costs
ideas.next: Desk research: what do Premiere, Resolve, Descript and the AI-first editing tools already do? Then ask three videographers how they log a wedding today.

ideas.name: Burned-in subtitles to editable .srt
ideas.pitch: Turn a video with hard-coded subtitles back into an editable subtitle file, for indie filmmakers, translators and festival submissions.
ideas.verdict: You've already built it once (Tomma Händer). The problem is real but occasional, which may make it better as a free tool that builds an audience than as a product people pay for.
edge: Working ffmpeg + OCR + cleanup pipeline
risks: Low willingness to pay
Free OCR tools already exist, at lower quality
ideas.next: Check existing tools and their quality. Consider releasing it free as an audience-builder.

ideas.name: Bespoke event and trip microsites
ideas.pitch: Memorable private sites for bachelorettes, weddings, reunions and birthdays: schedules, inside jokes, secret gates, slideshows.
ideas.verdict: Fun, fast to sell to friends-of-friends, and a strong portfolio. It's a want, not a pain, so it's priced as a gift. It probably won't scale beyond word of mouth.
edge: Emma bachelorette, Trung Thu and the Callback CV as a portfolio
risks: Wedding website builders (Zola, The Knot, Joy) are free
Every site is custom work, so it's hard to scale
ideas.next: Ask everyone who saw the Emma site whether they'd have paid for one, and how much.

ideas.name: Tết as a guest in a Vietnamese village
ideas.pitch: Small groups of westerners spend Tết as guests of a real family in the countryside: wrapping bánh chưng, the market run, lì xì. Like being brought home for midsommar.
ideas.verdict: This is access, not an itinerary, and access is what can't be copied. The hard part is keeping it organic: guests, not tourists, with roles to play, paying hosts properly, small groups, saying no often. It only happens once a year, so it's a premium experience, not an income. It doubles as writing material.
edge: Family and village access
You can brief guests on both cultures
The festival happens regardless, so it's authentic by default
risks: Feeling commercial ruins it for both hosts and guests
Once a year, with a hard deadline
Liability, transport and host-family consent
Tết is also the most expensive and crowded time to travel
ideas.next: Tết 2027 is 6 Feb. Run a free or at-cost pilot with 2–4 friends or colleagues, document it, and ask them afterwards what they would have paid.

ideas.name: Custom Vietnam itineraries
ideas.pitch: Tailored, exclusive itineraries for westerners in or visiting Vietnam.
ideas.verdict: AI makes generic itineraries free, and agencies and bloggers already cover this. It only survives as an add-on to something exclusive, like the Tết village.
edge: Local knowledge
risks: ChatGPT is the competitor
Sales and marketing heavy, which you said is your weak spot
ideas.next: Park it. Fold the useful parts into the Tết idea.

ideas.name: Build in public (the viral engine)
ideas.pitch: Share the weird, specific things you build with AI. The audience becomes the distribution channel for every other idea.
ideas.verdict: Not a business on its own, but it solves the sales problem that every other idea has. Score it as an enabler, not a money-maker.
edge: A backlog of real, shareable builds
risks: Time sink with no guarantee
Exposure while still employed
ideas.next: Pick one platform and one format. Post the drill-beat wedding cut story as the first test.

ideas.name: "Am I allowed?" assistant for co-op apartments
ideas.pitch: Upload or pick your bostadsrättsförening's bylaws and renovation rules. Describe what you want to do (new bathroom, move a wall, change pipes) and get what you can do yourself, what needs board approval, what needs a certified pro, and a ready-to-send application.
ideas.verdict: A real Swedish pain with no obvious owner after a first search. The 2023 change to the bostadsrättslag made more work need board consent, and renovating without it can mean restoring the apartment or even losing it. Rules differ per association, which is exactly what an AI reading your own documents handles well. Main open question: who pays, the member once per renovation, or the association or its manager to cut board workload?
edge: Swedish, and you live in a bostadsrätt yourself (you've just dealt with a board over subletting)
Builds on the home-repair research: Elsäkerhetsverket and wet-room rules feed the 'needs a pro' answers
Bylaws and renovation guidelines are often public on each association's website, so documents are easy to get for a demo

competitors.who: Boappa (owned by SBAB), HSB and Riksbyggen member portals
competitors.note: Communication, booking, fault reports and documents. No sign of an AI that interprets the rules or drafts the renovation application, but Boappa could add one, and it already sits inside many associations.

competitors.who: Lawline Q&A, Bostadsrätterna, HSB guidelines, boio.se guides
competitors.note: General answers about the law, not your association's specific rules.

competitors.who: HSB, Riksbyggen, SBC, Nabo and similar
competitors.note: Handle applications for many associations today; a possible customer or a channel rather than only a competitor.

risks: Boappa or the big managers add this as a feature
Legal-advice liability if the answer is wrong and the member renovates without consent
A once-per-renovation need: consumers rarely come back, so a B2B channel (associations, managers) may matter more
Getting each association's documents is manual unless the board or manager provides them
ideas.next: Collect bylaws and renovation guidelines from 10 associations (many are public), check how much they actually differ, then ask 3 board members how many renovation questions they handle per year and how long each takes.
market: Since 1 Jan 2023 the bostadsrättslag lists more measures that need board consent, including work on load-bearing structures.
The board can refuse only if the work causes 'påtaglig skada eller olägenhet' and can attach conditions. Members can appeal to Hyresnämnden.
Starting without consent can mean having to restore the apartment, and renovating despite a refusal can lead to losing the right to the apartment.
A municipal building permit does not replace board consent.

sources.label: Fastighetsägarna: when board consent is needed
Lawline: when the board can refuse a renovation
Dagens PS: renovating can cost you the apartment

ideas.name: AI SEO: getting found by ChatGPT, not just Google
ideas.pitch: Courses and audits that teach small businesses and marketers how to show up in AI answers (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews), also called GEO, generative engine optimization.
ideas.verdict: The pain is real and measurable: where Google shows an AI summary, clicks to websites drop by roughly 35-60% depending on the study. But English-language GEO courses are already everywhere, from free ones to about $300, and tracking tools start at about $25/month. The field is also young: nobody can yet prove which tactics work, so a course risks selling guesses. The gap after a first search is local: no Swedish-language course or hands-on offer for small Swedish firms turned up. The strongest form may be a fixed-price 'what does ChatGPT say about your business?' audit, sold as an add-on to the AI adoption workshop, with a course built later from what the audits teach. First hand audit (5 Stockholm businesses, 3 engines) found something worth showing every owner, but the fixes were mostly basic (publish prices, keep listings consistent), which points to selling the audit and a quarterly re-check rather than a GEO course.
edge: Swedish, for a local market the English courses don't serve
Pairs naturally with the AI adoption idea: same buyers, same first meeting
You build sites and already think about how crawlers read them (the robots.txt setup for this repo is the same knowledge, used the other way round)

competitors.who: Coursera (AI SEO: Mastering GEO), many Udemy courses, Trust Insights Academy, Search Engine Land/SMX master classes, BrightonSEO
competitors.note: Roughly $67-300 per course, plus free ones (GEO Academy, FreeAcademy.ai, a free Udemy course). Almost all in English, a few in German.

competitors.who: Profound, Otterly.ai, Peec AI, Rankscale, Airefs, RankAI
competitors.note: Monitor how often a brand is named in AI answers. Entry plans about $20-50/month, Profound is enterprise-priced. They sell the measurement; a course or audit sells the 'what now'.

competitors.who: Existing Swedish SEO and digital agencies adding 'AI search' to their offer
competitors.note: Have the clients already. The likely biggest competitor locally, and also a possible buyer of training.

ideas.pricing: GEO courses: $67-300 for paid online ones, many free. Tracking tools: about $25/month (Otterly) up to $500+/month (Peec AI's top plan, Profound). Prices come from vendor and comparison blogs, so check before relying on them.
market: A randomized 2026 study (Agarwal & Sen, not yet peer reviewed) found AI Overviews cut outbound clicks by 39.8%.
Ahrefs (Feb 2026): the top-ranked page gets 58% fewer clicks on keywords that show an AI Overview.
Chartbeat publisher data, as reported: Google search referrals down about 40% year on year (Jul 2025 to Jul 2026).
Counter-signal: one study (Amsive) found branded searches with an AI Overview get more clicks, not fewer. Being the named brand matters more than ranking.

Own audit (13 Nov 2026), 10 Swedish buyer questions × ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini: engines rarely agree. 'Best hairdresser on Södermalm' gave 10 salons with zero overlap; only 2 businesses were named by all three.
Own audit: firms that publish a fixed price on their site get quoted with it and often listed first (Plumber D, Video studio B, Lilla Ekonomibyrån, Midnatt Media).

Own audit: a salon with no prices online got 'no price list found, call them' from ChatGPT and an unsourced price list from Gemini. ChatGPT also misread an accounting firm's price tiers and volunteered its revenue and loss.
risks: No proven playbook yet: tactics are guesses that change as the models change. Teach how to measure and test, not a fixed recipe.
Crowded and cheap in English, so only the Swedish/local angle has room
SEO has a snake-oil reputation; promising results you can't measure would hurt
Knowledge goes stale even faster than AI tool tips
ideas.next: Turn one audit (salon C or accounting firm E) into a one-page report and show it to the owner or a small-business friend: what would they pay for it, and for a quarterly re-check? See research/ai-seo-audit.md.

ideas.name: Niche news, summarized and made funny
ideas.pitch: AI does the reading and summarizing; you add the angle and the jokes. A short daily or weekly digest of news for one specific audience, written like a stand-up set rather than a briefing.
ideas.verdict: Plain news summaries are a dead end: AI summaries are now free inside Google, Apple, Perplexity and every news app. What AI can't do well yet is be funny with a point of view, so the value is the voice, and the summarizing is just the cheap back end. That makes it a writing project first and a business second: money comes from ads and paid tiers once there's an audience, usually after many months. The niche question decides everything. Candidates: Swedish news explained with jokes for internationals and the Vietnamese community; a single beat (AI industry, Stockholm tech, Vietnam) done as satire; or the week's news as a short stand-up video. Best treated as an enabler that feeds the comedy workshop and build-in-public, unless one niche shows it can pay.
edge: The comedy workshop: you're already practising writing jokes and have a method for it
Swedish and Vietnamese: you can explain one culture's news to the other, a niche few can cover
Comfortable automating the boring half (collect, summarize, rank stories) with AI

competitors.who: Morning Brew, The Skimm, Axios, Semafor
competitors.note: Witty general news briefings with large teams. Not worth competing with head-on.

competitors.who: Google AI Overviews, Apple Intelligence notification summaries, Perplexity Discover, Particle and similar news apps
competitors.note: Make 'just a summary' worth zero. The reason the product has to be the voice.

competitors.who: The Onion, late-night TV clips, and a long tail of small AI-made satire newsletters (TheDailyPoop, We Interrupt This Reality, Koo AI)
competitors.note: The small AI satire projects show low traction: the jokes feel generated. A human comic voice is the gap.

competitors.who: The Local Sweden (paid membership), SVT/SR news in English and easy Swedish
competitors.note: Serves the 'Sweden explained' niche straight, not funny. Nothing obvious in Vietnamese.

ideas.pricing: Newsletter platforms report paid subscriptions growing fast, driven by niche writers (beehiiv: $19M paid revenue in 2025, up from $8M; self-reported). A common rule of thumb is that 2-5% of a free list converts to a paid tier of about $5-10/month, so 10,000 free readers is roughly 200-500 paying. Ads and sponsorships usually matter more early on.
market: Generalist newsletters face heavy competition; platforms say growth is in narrow niches with a clear audience.
Many small AI-made satire and digest newsletters exist, but none in the search showed real traction, which suggests generated humour alone doesn't hold readers.
risks: Slow money: an audience first, revenue months or years later
Daily output is a treadmill; weekly is more realistic next to a job and the Vietnam stint
Comedy about news can offend, and some niches (politics, the diaspora) are sensitive
AI writing jokes will get better, so the human voice must be genuinely distinct
Exposure while still employed (same as build in public)
ideas.next: Pick one niche and write four weekly issues by hand (AI for gathering and summarizing, you for the jokes). Send them to 20 people from the right audience and count how many open the third and fourth, and how many forward one.
